paper_metadata.title: Phase inversion in a lightweight high Al content refractory high-entropy alloy

evidence.quote: Adding Al is an important strategy to obtain ultrahigh specific strength in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). However, the main structure typically transitions from disordered BCC to ordered B2 with increasing Al concentration, leading to poor ductility.

An alloy with a nominal composition of Zr40Ti28Nb12Al20 was produced by induction melting and mixing high-purity metals (≥ 99.9% weight percent, wt.%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted at least ten times and solidified in a water-cooled crucible with a diameter of 150 mm and height of 300 mm.
Subsequently, the as-cast sample was homogenized at 1473 K for 2 h followed by water quenching
and then warm-rolled at 923 K to reach a thickness reduction of 50%.
The rolled samples were then isothermally annealed at 923 K for 6, 12, 18, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 and 60 min
and isochronally annealed at 923, 973, 1023 and 1073 K for 30 min followed by air-cooling.

Notably, the addition of Al not only reduces the density, but can also significantly improve the strength due to solid solution hardening as there is a large elastic and atomic size misfits between Al and most transition metals (TMs).
Similar to the structure of Ni-based superalloys, the continuous soft (BCC) matrix provides good ductility, while the hard (B2) precipitates enable very high strength by precipitation hardening.
